argument.issue: Did the Agency err in finding an interchange at Coutts, Alberta?
argument.claim: There was no interchange at Coutts because BNSF did not have a line of railway there under Agency jurisdiction.
argument.quote: CP argued that there was no interchange at Coutts, Alberta because BNSF did not have a line of railway there which connected with CP’s railway in Canada so as to be subject to the Agency’s jurisdiction.

support.ref: railway line as 'single and seamless' at boundary

argument.weak_spot: The other side may argue BNSF's contractual rights or physical presence suffice for jurisdiction.

best_match.quoted_paragraph: In conclusion, it is our view that the Board’s finding that the employees engaged in its charter airline and air ambulance services were employed in the operation of a federal work, undertaking or business, within the meaning of section 2 of the Code, is supportable on the basis of the record.

argument.issue: What is the standard of review for the Agency’s determination of jurisdiction over BNSF?
argument.claim: The Agency’s determination of jurisdiction is a true question of jurisdiction, reviewable on a correctness standard.
argument.quote: CP argues, however, that the Agency’s determination that BNSF has a line of railway which extends into Canada such that the Agency has authority over BNSF is a true question of jurisdiction, in respect of which the standard of review is correctness.
argument.weak_spot: The other side may argue the issue is one of mixed fact and law, attracting reasonableness review.

argument.issue: Did the Agency rely on improper or insufficient evidence regarding the connection between railway lines?
argument.claim: The Agency improperly relied on an intervener’s brief from another proceeding as evidentiary foundation for its finding.
argument.quote: CP was particularly critical of the Agency’s apparent reliance on a passage taken from an intervener’s brief in another proceeding... CP infers that the citation is the evidentiary foundation for the Agency’s statement.
argument.weak_spot: The other side may argue the Agency had other evidence or that the passage was not determinative.

best_match.quoted_paragraph: With the only possible exception of the negative credibility inference regarding the First Information Report, the Court is of the opinion that the RPD’s negative plausibility findings are reasonable as they are intertwined with numerous adverse credibility conclusions which are supported by reliable and a verifiable evidentiary based reasons, made with regard to the Applicants’ milieu.

argument.issue: Did the Agency misinterpret its own and the Court’s jurisprudence regarding what constitutes a 'line of railway'?
argument.claim: The Agency misinterpreted Fort Rouge and departed from its own jurisprudence by treating contractual rights as sufficient for a 'line of railway'.
argument.quote: CP’s position is that the Agency departed from its own jurisprudence and misinterpreted this Court’s decision in Fort Rouge when it held that the mere contractual rights... gave BNSF a sufficient interest in the Coutts Yard to allow it to treat the Coutts Yard as part of its line of railway.
argument.weak_spot: The other side may argue Fort Rouge supports a broader interpretation of 'line of railway' including contractual rights.

argument.issue: Are BNSF’s rights under the Interchange Agreement sufficient to constitute a 'line of railway'?
argument.claim: BNSF’s rights under the Interchange Agreement are less than those in Celgar and Fort Rouge, and thus insufficient for a 'line of railway'.
argument.quote: CP says that BNSF’s rights under the Interchange Agreement are more like BN’s rights under the agreement in issue in Celgar. CP also points out that BN had more than 'mere' running rights under that agreement.
argument.weak_spot: The other side may argue the rights under the Interchange Agreement are sufficient for jurisdiction or are distinguishable from Celgar.
